data.title: Xeroderma pigmentosum — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Xeroderma pigmentosum** (Genodermatoses)_

**Q1. What is xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)?**
- Rare autosomal recessive disorder of nucleotide excision repair (NER) of UV-induced DNA damage (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, 6-4 photoproducts) — complementation groups XPA–XPG and variant (XPV — POLH, defective translesion synthesis); commoner with consanguinity (India, Middle East, Japan)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Infancy: acute exaggerated sunburn on minimal exposure (in ~50% — XPA, XPB, XPD, XPF, XPG), photophobia
- Early childhood: freckling (lentigines) on sun-exposed skin by 2 years, xerosis, poikiloderma (atrophy, telangiectasia, mottled hyper/hypopigmentation)
- Skin cancers: >10,000-fold risk of NMSC before 20 years (median age of first NMSC ~9 y) and ~2000-fold melanoma risk; also tongue tip SCC
- Eyes: photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, ectropion, corneal clouding, ocular surface tumours
- Neurological (~25%, XPA, XPD): progressive neurodegeneration — sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, areflexia, ataxia, intellectual decline; De Sanctis–Cacchione syndrome (XP + dwarfism, hypogonadism, severe neurological)
- Internal malignancies: CNS tumours, leukaemia, lung

**Q3. Enumerate disorders caused by defective DNA repair (PYQ).**
- Xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome (cachectic dwarfism, photosensitivity without cancer, pigmentary retinopathy — ERCC6/8), trichothiodystrophy (brittle sulphur-deficient hair with tiger-tail banding under polarised light — PIBIDS), XP–Cockayne overlap, UV-sensitive syndrome, Bloom syndrome (BLM helicase — photosensitive malar telangiectatic erythema, short stature, immunodeficiency, cancers; high sister chromatid exchange), Rothmund–Thomson (RECQL4 — poikiloderma from infancy, sparse hair, skeletal defects, osteosarcoma), Werner syndrome (adult progeria — WRN), ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM), Fanconi anaemia, dyskeratosis congenita (telomere maintenance), Muir–Torre/Lynch (mismatch repair)

**Q4. Write a short note on Rothmund–Thomson and Bloom syndromes (PYQ).**
- Rothmund–Thomson (poikiloderma congenitale): AR RECQL4; erythema and blistering of cheeks at 3–6 months spreading to extremities → poikiloderma, sparse hair/eyebrows, juvenile cataracts, short stature, radial ray defects, dental anomalies; osteosarcoma and skin cancers
- Bloom: AR BLM; growth retardation, narrow face, photosensitive butterfly telangiectatic erythema, CALMs, immunodeficiency, infertility, very high risk of leukaemia/lymphoma and other cancers early in life

**Q5. Diagnosis.**
- Clinical; DNA repair assays — unscheduled DNA synthesis in cultured fibroblasts after UV, host-cell reactivation, comet assay; post-UV cell survival; molecular genetic testing for the complementation group; prenatal diagnosis possible

**Q6. Management.**
- Rigorous lifelong UV protection: avoid daylight (night activities — 'children of the night'), UV-protective clothing, face shields, UV-blocking films on windows, broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreens, sunglasses; vitamin D supplementation
- Skin surveillance every 3–6 months by dermatologist; early excision of premalignant/malignant lesions; field therapy (5-FU, imiquimod), PDT; oral retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin) for chemoprevention; nicotinamide; T4 endonuclease V liposome lotion (experimental)
- Eye: methylcellulose drops, protective eyewear; neurological and audiological follow-up; genetic counselling
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors highly effective for advanced cancers in XP (high mutational burden)

**Q7. Describe the genetic complementation groups.**
- Autosomal recessive defects of nucleotide excision repair (NER): XP-A to XP-G (XPA — severe neurological disease, Japan; XPC — commonest worldwide, no neurology; XPD — overlaps with trichothiodystrophy/Cockayne), plus XP variant (POLH — translesion DNA polymerase η, normal NER, milder, adult onset)

**Q8. What cancers develop and at what age?**
- Median age of first NMSC ~9 years (vs ~60 in general population) — BCC, SCC, melanoma (≈ 2000-fold risk for NMSC, 2000× melanoma before age 20); ocular (conjunctival SCC, corneal clouding), tongue tip SCC; internal cancers (CNS, lung, leukaemia) somewhat increased

**Q9. Neurological features.**
- In ~25% (mainly XPA, XPD): progressive sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, intellectual decline, ataxia, areflexia, peripheral neuropathy — De Sanctis–Cacchione syndrome (with dwarfism and hypogonadism)

**Q10. Explain nucleotide excision repair and why its defect causes skin cancer.**
- UV (mainly UVB) produces cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts in DNA; NER recognises (XPC, XPE), unwinds (XPB, XPD — TFIIH), excises (XPG, XPF–ERCC1) the damaged segment and polymerase fills the gap
- Defect → unrepaired UV lesions → C→T and CC→TT 'UV signature' mutations in p53, PTCH1, oncogenes → early skin cancers; neurons (oxidative DNA damage repaired by NER) degenerate → neurological disease

**Q11. Describe the cutaneous course of XP.**
- Severe sunburn on minimal exposure in ~50% (XPA, XPD) from infancy; others show early freckling (by age 2) without burning (XPC, XPE)
- Progressive photoageing: xerosis, poikiloderma (hypo/hyperpigmentation, telangiectasia, atrophy), actinic keratoses, keratoacanthomas, BCC, SCC, melanoma (lentigo maligna) in childhood on face, lips, tip of tongue

**Q12. Ocular involvement.**
- Photophobia, conjunctivitis, keratitis, corneal opacification, ectropion, loss of eyelashes, conjunctival/ corneal SCC and melanoma of exposed eye; protection with UV-blocking glasses, lubricants

**Q13. How is XP diagnosed?**
- Clinical features + cellular tests: unscheduled DNA synthesis (UDS) in cultured fibroblasts after UV, UV-sensitivity/ host-cell reactivation assays, recovery of RNA synthesis; molecular genetic testing (complementation group); prenatal diagnosis possible

**Q14. Photoprotection measures in XP (practical).**
- Avoid all daylight UV — stay indoors in daytime, UV-blocking films on windows and car glass, UV meters, protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats with UV-protective face shields, gloves, high SPF broad-spectrum sunscreens reapplied, wrap-around UV sunglasses; 'children of the night' — schooling arrangements
- Vitamin D supplementation (deficiency due to sun avoidance)

**Q15. Treatment of skin lesions in XP.**
- Frequent (3–6 monthly) full-skin examinations; early excision of suspicious lesions (Mohs for facial tumours), cryotherapy/ curettage for small lesions; field therapy for AKs — 5-FU, imiquimod, PDT (caution), chemical peels/ dermabrasion; oral retinoids (isotretinoin/ acitretin) for chemoprevention; nicotinamide; T4 endonuclease V liposome lotion (experimental); immunotherapy (PD-1 inhibitors) for advanced cancers — XP tumours respond well (high mutation burden); radiotherapy can be used when needed (repair of ionising-radiation damage is intact) but with caution

**Q16. Differentiate XP from other photosensitive genodermatoses.**
- Cockayne syndrome (CSA/CSB — photosensitivity without increased cancer, cachectic dwarfism, 'bird-like' face, progeria, cataracts, retinal pigmentation, neurodegeneration)
- Trichothiodystrophy (XPD/TTDN1 — brittle sulphur-deficient hair with 'tiger-tail' banding on polarised light, ichthyosis, intellectual disability, photosensitivity, no cancer increase)
- Bloom syndrome (BLM — telangiectatic facial erythema, short stature, immunodeficiency, cancers — leukaemia), Rothmund–Thomson (RECQL4 — poikiloderma from infancy, skeletal defects, osteosarcoma), porphyrias (EPP — burning pain), Hartnup disease, Kindler syndrome

**Q17. Genetic counselling in XP.**
- Autosomal recessive — 25% recurrence; high in consanguineous communities (India, Middle East, North Africa); carrier testing for siblings; prenatal diagnosis

**Q18. Prognosis.**
- Without protection, median survival historically ~32 years (mainly metastatic skin cancer, neurological degeneration); strict photoprotection from early childhood markedly reduces cancers

**Q19. What is the De Sanctis–Cacchione syndrome?**
- Severe XP (usually XPA) with microcephaly, progressive intellectual disability, dwarfism, hypogonadism, sensorineural deafness, spasticity/ ataxia — neurological XP

**Q20. XP variant — how is it different?**
- Defect in DNA polymerase η (POLH) for translesion synthesis; NER normal; milder, later onset (2nd–4th decade) skin cancers, no neurological disease; cellular test — UV sensitivity in presence of caffeine

**Q21. Role of dermatology team in school and social life.**
- Educate teachers/ family, organise indoor activities, UV-safe classrooms (film on windows, LED lighting low-UV), psychological support, support groups ('XP Family Support')

**Q22. Internal and other cancers in XP.**
- ~10–20 fold increased internal cancers — CNS tumours (gliomas), lung (smokers), haematological (leukaemia), thyroid; avoid smoking and other carcinogens

**Q23. What anaesthesia/ procedural precautions?**
- Light sources in operating theatres and surgical lamps can emit UV — use filters/ LED; minimise fluorescent exposure; ophthalmic procedures need UV protection

**Q24. Why are lip, tongue tip and eyes common tumour sites?**
- Highly sun-exposed mucosal sites without melanin protection and with frequent UV exposure (lower lip, anterior tongue, conjunctiva/ cornea) — SCC of tongue tip is almost exclusive to XP in children

**Q25. Chemopreventive retinoid regimen.**
- Isotretinoin 0.5–2 mg/kg/day reduced new skin cancers by ~60% in XP (Kraemer study) but with significant toxicity; lower doses (0.5 mg/kg) or acitretin used; tumours recur on stopping — long-term use with monitoring

## Quick spotter facts
- Freckling and poikiloderma with multiple skin cancers in a child of consanguineous parents — XP (NER defect)
- Children of the night — strict UV protection

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of DNA repair). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
